summary: Describes using Segment Routing to scale networks to hundreds of thousands of nodes and tens of millions of endpoints, such as interconnected large data centers. Midpoint and leaf nodes need only modest forwarding tables. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A way to guide traffic through a gigantic network where each router remembers only a small amount, like following a travel itinerary.

subtitle: Scaling networks to hundreds of thousands of nodes with efficient routing

tldr.problem: Large networks with millions of endpoints need routing protocols that do not require every router to maintain massive forwarding tables with millions of entries.
tldr.mechanism: Segment Routing uses a hierarchical design where each domain allocates unique segment identifier ranges, and routers maintain only a few tens of thousands of entries by using path compression and anycast segments.
tldr.outcome: Networks can interconnect hundreds of thousands of nodes and tens of millions of endpoints while keeping midpoint and leaf node forwarding tables modest.

today: RFC 8604 is Informational and remains the primary reference for scaling networks with Segment Routing. It has not been obsoleted, and the design patterns it describes continue to guide large-scale network deployments, especially in data center interconnection.

sections.title: Scaling with Segment Routing
sections.content:
RFC 8604 describes a practical application of Segment Routing (SR) to build and operate networks at massive scale. The design supports hundreds of thousands of network nodes and tens of millions of physical endpoints, which makes it suitable for interconnecting large data centers or building massive aggregation networks.

The key insight is that forwarding tables of midpoint and leaf nodes can remain small (a few tens of thousands of entries) even when the network as a whole has millions of nodes, because routers use segment-based forwarding and the inherently scalable nature of Segment Routing design.
sections.plainLanguage: You can build a network with millions of computers where each router only remembers a small list of important waypoints instead of knowing how to reach every single computer.

sections.title: Reference Design
sections.content:
The RFC proposes a hierarchical design with independent routing domains: a core (C) domain with 200 nodes, metro (M) regions (M1 and M2), and data centers (DC1 and DC2). Each region runs its own Segment Routing instance (ISIS or OSPF with SR extensions), and a shared homogeneous Segment Routing Global Block (SRGB) of 16000-23999 is used throughout.

Unique SRGB sub-ranges are allocated to each domain: core gets 16000-16999, Metro1 gets 17000-17999, and Metro2 gets 18000-18999. Inside each data center, the same range (20000-23999) is reused. Aggregation node routes are redistributed between domains, but no other routes are advertised across domain boundaries.
sections.plainLanguage: The network is divided into regions, and each region has its own phone book of addresses. There is a master list that is the same everywhere, so routers can talk between regions.

sections.title: Design Options and Scaling
sections.content:
The design supports several scaling techniques. With the reference topology (100 leaf domains, each with 6,000 leaf-node segments and 500 adjacency segments per node), the network reaches 600,000 nodes and 300 million endpoints. A leaf node in this design maintains only 6,800 segments (6,000 leaf-node segments, 300 core-node segments, 500 adjacency segments), while a core node maintains 6,300 segments.

Path compression further reduces the burden: intermediate routing policies are assigned binding segment identifiers, so a path expressed as {16001, 16002, 16003, 18006, 20001} can be compressed to {16001, 4001, 20001} where 4001 is a binding SID that encodes the middle segments. When core topology changes, the control plane updates only the middle segment, not the end-to-end path at every node.
sections.plainLanguage: By grouping many small paths into a single shortcut, routers remember less while still knowing how to send traffic everywhere. When the network changes, you only fix the shortcut, not every path through it.

sections.title: Control Plane and Traffic Engineering
sections.content:
A Path Computation Element (PCE) computes Segment Routing Traffic Engineering (SRTE) policies on demand. When a node needs to reach a remote node with specific service-level requirements (such as low-latency or disjointness from other services), it sends a PCEP request to the PCE. The PCE maintains a multi-domain topology fed by BGP-LS updates and computes the path as a segment list.

The control plane programs the source node with an SRTE policy, which then steers pseudowires and other traffic into that policy. Because each segment in the list is optimized for Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP), the entire policy load-shares across available paths automatically.
sections.plainLanguage: A central traffic controller figures out the best route based on what matters (speed, avoiding broken parts) and tells the start node to use that route. The routers in between automatically share the load.

sections.title: Benefits and Deployment
sections.content:
The design eliminates the need for LDP (Label Distribution Protocol) and RSVP-TE, reducing protocol complexity. It supports inter-domain service-level agreements with fast reroute and resiliency through Topology Independent Loop-Free Alternate (TI-LFA), achieving sub-50-millisecond reroute times on link, node, or Shared Risk Link Group failures.

The design is suitable for both green field (new) and brown field (migrating from existing MPLS) deployments. Because every Segment Routing policy is expressed as a list of segments and each segment is optimized for ECMP, the entire end-to-end policy naturally load-shares across available paths without per-flow state at midpoints.
sections.plainLanguage: You do not need extra protocols just to remember which routes to use. Routers can automatically split traffic evenly, and if one part breaks, traffic finds another way almost instantly.
